project.title: Release eval - Brackenridge graded foam filters

sections.s242:
It was uncertain whether a two-zone template with a 10 ppi entry and 30 ppi exit could survive firing without delamination, because slurry loading per strut varies across the part and the outcome could not be calculated. Dunmore Falls Ceramics is a manufacturer of foam-ceramic filters for metal foundries, and the team calls its graded structure the cascade-fired lattice. The company set out to make a filter that cracks less and catches more fine inclusions, so thin-wall customers get cleaner metal without slow filling. It has made sponge-replicated filters for over twenty years.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to build a graded filter from replicated foam was insufficient. Stacking two filters doubles the cost, and the gap between the pieces lets metal bypass. Thicker fine filters crack worse and prime harder. No documented methods existed for a replicated foam with a pore gradient through 50 mm fired at production scale; published graded foams were lab-scale and made by other methods. Shrinkage data existed only for uniform filters.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of firing shrinkage matching, fine-inclusion capture versus flow, and thermal shock behaviour in sponge-replicated foam with a pore-size gradient, for the purpose of producing a graded filter for aluminium casting. The team sought to learn whether a two-zone template would survive firing without delamination.

The team did not know if the shrinkage mismatch would tear the part apart at the interface. It was uncertain whether interface stress could be predicted, because the struts are hollow after burnout and interface stress could not be modelled well. It was also uncertain whether the graded filter could raise capture of 20 to 80 micron inclusions while holding flow and priming head near the standard 20 ppi filter, and whether the interface would stop or start cracks under thermal shock.
sections.s244:
The technological problem was whether a sponge-replicated alumina foam with a 10 ppi entry zone and a 30 ppi exit zone could survive firing without delamination, because slurry loading per strut varies across the part. The team planned the work in August 2025 in three phases, covering the uncertainties stated in Line 242. Phase 1 made graded green bodies that survive firing, to test the shrinkage mismatch at the interface. Phase 2 measured flow and fine-inclusion capture on the survivors. Phase 3 ran thermal shock and burst tests, then a pour trial at a customer foundry.

It was hypothesized that if a 10 ppi and 30 ppi two-zone template carries matched slurry mass per volume, then linear firing shrinkage across the interface will stay within 0.5 percent and the part will survive firing without delamination. The graded filter should then capture at least 30 percent more 20 to 80 micron inclusions than the standard 20 ppi filter, at a flow rate no more than 10 percent lower. Results outside these thresholds would disprove it.

The team did not know if the shrinkage mismatch would tear the part apart at the interface, so trial 1 (September 2025) bonded 10 ppi and 30 ppi sponge sheets (25 mm each) with polyurethane adhesive. It used a single dip in standard alumina slurry (about 2,400 mPa.s). Firing was standard (1,580 C peak, 2 h hold) on 24 filters of 75x75x50 mm. Delamination at the bond line affected 18 of 24 parts. On the survivors, the 30 ppi side shrank 1.4 percent more than the 10 ppi side. The finer sponge picked up more slurry per volume, and the adhesive left a burnout gap. The team concluded that unequal slurry pick-up is linked to the mismatch and that adhesive bonding is not viable.

Trial 2 (October-November 2025) fused the sponges thermally instead of using adhesive and applied a two-stage dip: the whole part in about 1,500 mPa.s slurry, then only the coarse half in 2,400 mPa.s slurry. Delamination fell to 9 of 40 parts and the shrinkage mismatch to 0.7 percent, still above the 0.5 percent target. Equalising slurry mass per volume helped but did not close the gap alone.

Trial 3 (December 2025-January 2026) kept the two-stage dip and added a slow ramp of 1 C per minute between 1,100 and 1,350 C, with a 45 minute hold at 1,350 C. Only 2 of 36 parts delaminated, and the shrinkage mismatch measured 0.4 percent, within target. The extra kiln time was about 3 hours per load. The team concluded that mismatch is driven more by slurry mass per volume than by pore size, and that a slow ramp through the sintering window absorbs the remaining difference.

Trial 4 (February 2026) tested capture and flow on a rig using 50 kg of A356 per run at 720 C, with 6 pours each of the standard 20 ppi, standard 30 ppi and graded filter (25 mm fine zone). The 20 ppi filter gave about 4.1 kg/s; the 30 ppi gave 2.9 kg/s with a 30 percent higher priming head. The graded filter gave 3.8 kg/s, 7 percent below the 20 ppi, and captured 41 percent more inclusions, meeting both targets. In 2 of 6 graded pours, however, the fine side choked near the end. Trial 5 (March 2026) reduced the fine exit layer to 15 mm over 8 pours. Flow held at 3.9 kg/s across the full 50 kg with no choking, and capture was 36 percent above the 20 ppi. The team chose the 15 mm layer.

Trial 6 (April 2026) asked whether the interface would stop or start cracks. After quenching from 700 C into room-temperature water, retained strength was about 55 percent for the standard 20 ppi and 68 percent for the graded filter. In burst tests with a 300 mm head, 3 of 20 standard 50 mm filters cracked, against 1 of 20 graded filters, where the crack stopped at the interface. Of 10 retained trial 2 parts, which had higher mismatch, 4 cracked along the interface. A well-matched interface therefore arrested cracks, while a poorly matched one became the failure plane.
sections.s246:
The team did not know if the shrinkage mismatch would tear the part apart at the interface, and trial 3 resolved that question: the mismatch measured 0.4 percent against the 0.5 percent limit, with 2 of 36 parts showing delamination. The technological objective was to advance understanding of shrinkage matching, fine-inclusion capture versus flow, and thermal shock behaviour in sponge-replicated foam with a pore-size gradient. The hypothesis was partly proven. The graded filter also met the capture and flow targets in trial 4: 41 percent more inclusions captured, with flow 7 percent below the 20 ppi filter.

Shrinkage mismatch tracks slurry mass per volume more than pore size. Based on this, the team adopted a two-stage dip and a slow ramp of 1 C per minute between 1,100 and 1,350 C, which absorbed the remaining difference. Adhesive bonding is not viable because it burns out before the ceramic sinters. Trial 1 confirmed this: 18 of 24 parts delaminated at the bond line, and thermal fusing replaced adhesive.

A well-matched interface arrests cracks, while a poorly matched one becomes the failure plane. In trial 6, retained strength was 68 percent for the graded filter against 55 percent for the standard 20 ppi filter. Fine exit layer thickness also governs choking: a 25 mm layer choked in 2 of 6 pours, while a 15 mm layer held 3.9 kg/s with capture 36 percent above the 20 ppi filter.

The open question is whether the graded filter works at 30 mm thickness, the highest volume format. It remains uncertain because shrinkage and choking behaviour were established only at 50 mm. The planned approach is to repeat the two-stage dip and ramp work at 30 mm.

The project goal was a graded filter that cracks less and captures more fine inclusions. The team could not tell whether mismatch would tear the part, and learned that a two-stage dip plus a slow ramp brings it under 0.5 percent.

project.title: Release eval - Marrowgate cold-water biofilter control

sections.s242:
The company designs recirculating aquaculture systems for land-based trout farms. It set out to give clients a faster, steadier cold-water biofilter, so trout farms can stock fish sooner. Clients' water is often 6 to 12 C. The company's pilot system has four independent loops, each with a 6 m3 fish tank and a 1.2 m3 moving bed biofilter.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to speed nitrification start-up below 10 C was insufficient. Start-up took 9 to 10 weeks at that temperature, against 3 to 4 weeks at 20 C. Standard practice relies on ammonium chloride dosing and waiting, or on seeding with media from an existing biofilter. Seeding from a warm system fails because seed media goes into shock in 8 degree water, and the bacteria survive but barely grow. No documented method existed for conditioning warm-system media for cold water.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of how nitrifying biofilm responds to temperature change in cold water, for the purpose of creating a moving bed biofilter start-up method. The target was cold-water start-up under 5 weeks at 8 C.

The open question was how to shorten nitrification start-up at water temperatures below 10 C. Seed media from a warm system goes into shock in 8 degree water, so it was uncertain whether stepwise acclimation could work. The planned approach cooled the seed 1 C every 4 days from 14 C to 8 C. It was unclear whether stepwise cooling would let the bacteria grow instead of barely surviving, because the response of nitrifiers in seed media to gradual cooling had not been documented. It was also unknown whether 10 percent was the right seed fraction, or whether the result would hold at 6 C.
sections.s244:
The open question was how to shorten nitrification start-up below 10 C, where seed media from a warm system risked shock and stepwise acclimation had never been shown to let nitrifiers grow. The team planned to test how to shorten nitrification start-up below 10 C on a four-loop pilot. Each loop had a 6 m3 tank and a 1.2 m3 moving bed biofilter. The company ran the start-up trials in fall and winter 2025, when intake water was naturally cold. Technicians ran the loops, did daily water chemistry and pulled samples. The lab ran total ammonia nitrogen, nitrite and alkalinity by standard wet chemistry. Full nitrification was defined as a loop taking 1 mg/L total ammonia nitrogen to under 0.2 mg/L in 24 hours with nitrite under 0.3 mg/L.

It was hypothesized that if seed media is acclimated stepwise, cooling 1 C every 4 days from 14 C to 8 C, and used as 10 percent of the media, then full nitrification at 8 C will take under 5 weeks. A result of 35 days or more would disprove it. Unacclimated seed and an unseeded loop served as baselines.

Experiment 1 addressed whether stepwise acclimation would let seed bacteria grow rather than barely survive at 8 C. The company ran three loops at 8 C from September to November 2025. Loop A had no seed and ammonium chloride dosing only. Loop B had 10 percent of its media replaced with mature media taken straight from a 16 C production system. Full nitrification took 66 days in Loop A and 47 days in Loop B, and Loop B stalled at the nitrite stage for almost three weeks. The stall suggests, but does not confirm, the cause of the slow start-up in warm seed. Loop C received 10 percent seed first acclimated in a side tank, dropping 1 C every 4 days from 14 C to 8 C. Loop C reached full nitrification in 31 days, under the 5-week target, with a nitrite stall of about 6 days. Stepwise acclimation therefore cut start-up at 8 C from 47 to 31 days compared with unacclimated seed.

Experiment 2 addressed whether the result would hold at 6 C and what seed fraction was needed. From January to February 2026 the company ran loops at 6 C with acclimated seed at 5 and 15 percent. The 5 percent loop took 44 days, which was over the 5-week target, so a low seed fraction did not carry the 8 C result to 6 C. The 15 percent loop took 29 days, under the target. The 10 percent fraction was not tested at 6 C, and each seed fraction was a single run. At 6 C, about 15 percent acclimated seed was needed to get under 5 weeks, and returns appeared to flatten above roughly 10 to 15 percent.
sections.s246:
Whether stepwise acclimation would let seed bacteria grow rather than barely survive in 8 C water was the open question. Through this investigation, it was established that stepwise acclimation of seed media lets the seeded biofilter reach full nitrification at 8 C in 31 days. The objective was a cold-water start-up under 5 weeks at 8 C, and the hypothesis was proven at 8 C. Full nitrification took 66 days in the unseeded loop and 47 days with unacclimated seed. Stepwise acclimation of seed media cut start-up at 8 C from 47 days to 31 days.

It was determined that stepwise acclimation of seed media roughly halves start-up time compared with unacclimated seed at 8 C. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether stepwise cooling would let the bacteria grow instead of barely surviving. sections.s242:
Early fault warning on grain dryers could not be given reliably, because it was unknown whether a model could separate slow sensor drift from slow real faults without labels. The team sought to learn whether the two differ in a way a model can use. The goal was a model that warns operators of burner and column faults early enough to act. The company builds controllers and analytics software for grain dryers. Its controllers read temperature and moisture sensors and run the burner and discharge rate, which gave the team field experience of how sensors behave over a harvest season.

Fixed-threshold alarms are late, because plenum temperature crosses the threshold only when the fault is well along. Drift-compensation methods in the literature mostly assume a trusted reference sensor or periodic calibration, and the dryers have neither. No documented method separated slow sensor drift from slow real faults, such as a plugging column, without labelled drift examples. Retraining on drifted data teaches a model that drift is normal, which can hide slow faults.

The technological objective was to advance understanding of anomaly detection on drifting, coupled industrial sensor data without labelled drift examples or reference sensors. The target was detecting burner and column faults with a median lead time of at least 15 minutes and fewer than 0.25 false alarms per dryer-day under sensor drift up to 3 °C per month.

It was uncertain whether a model could separate slow sensor drift from slow real faults without labels, because making a model tolerant of slow change also slows its detection of slow faults. It was uncertain whether bias could be separated from real process change in a coupled system, because burner output, air flow, grain flow, ambient conditions and grain moisture interact and only the available sensors could be used. It was uncertain whether anomaly scores on an energy balance residual, with online bias tracking from redundant sensors, would keep false alarms under target, particularly on dryers with one plenum sensor. It was also uncertain whether 11 documented faults could validate the approach.
sections.s244:
The technical problem was whether a model could separate slow sensor drift from real faults that also develop slowly, such as a plugging column, without labelled drift examples or a trusted reference sensor. The company planned the work in phases. It first rebuilt the isolation forest baseline and measured how it failed under injected drift. It then tested synthetic drift training, followed by an energy balance residual model with online bias tracking, and finally ran shadow mode trials on customer dryers. In July 2025, before any run, the team defined a false alarm as an alert with no fault in the following two hours, counted per dryer-day. Lead time ran from the alert to the earlier of the existing hard-limit alarm or the operator's manual shutdown. Fixing these definitions in advance kept the pass criteria from shifting with results.

It was hypothesized that if anomaly scores were computed on energy balance residuals with online bias tracking from redundant sensors, then false alarms per dryer-day would stay below 0.25 and median lead time would stay at or above 15 minutes under sensor drift up to 3 °C per month. Either measure missing its target on injected drift or shadow mode data would disprove the hypothesis.

Slow sensor drift could not be told from slow faults, so the team rebuilt the baseline. The rebuilt isolation forest on raw sensor readings had looked good in the lab, so the team injected drift to test it. At 3 °C per month it produced 2.6 false alarms per dryer-day with a median lead time of 9 minutes, missing both targets. The team concluded that raw readings could not carry the distinction. A model had to learn what drift looked like or have it removed. This result set the comparison point for later phases. The work also covered a billing portal migration to a new cloud host, which was routine IT work.

The next question was whether synthetic drift training could teach the model to ignore drift without hiding slow faults. The team trained with synthetic drift and replayed the 11 documented faults. False alarms fell to 0.6 per dryer-day, but the model caught only 6 of 11 faults and missed all three column plugs, which build over 30 to 60 minutes. The model had learned to treat slow rises as drift. The team dropped the approach, learning that tolerance to slow change and detection of slow faults trade against each other in this method.

The team then asked whether physics could separate the two. It computed an energy balance residual and tracked per-sensor bias online with a Kalman filter, using sensor redundancy. On injected drift this gave 0.18 false alarms per dryer-day, 10 of 11 faults and a median lead time of 22 minutes, meeting both targets. The shadow mode trial on nine customer dryers in fall 2025 showed a split. The seven dual-sensor dryers gave 0.21 false alarms per dryer-day, below the 0.25 limit, but the two single-sensor dryers gave 0.64. All four real events were flagged, with lead times of 14, 19, 26 and 31 minutes. The 14-minute flame event was below the 15-minute target. Without the redundant sensor, the bias tracker could not separate drift from process change and had to be set conservatively, so a fault was absorbed.

The team finally tested whether exhaust temperature could act as an indirect second reference on the single-sensor dryers. This cut false alarms from 0.64 to 0.33 per dryer-day, still above the 0.25 limit. Sensor redundancy therefore decides performance, and exhaust temperature only partly replaces it. Moisture sensor drift remains less well handled than temperature drift. The model continues to run in shadow mode on the same nine dryers. Whether 11 documented faults plus four real events suffice for validation is unresolved.
sections.s246:
Slow sensor drift and slow real faults were hard to tell apart without labels, and it was unknown whether a model could tolerate drift without losing detection of slow faults. Through this investigation, it was established that slow drift and slow faults were separated using energy balance residuals with online bias tracking, though the hypothesis was only partly proven. On injected drift of 3 °C per month, this gave 0.18 false alarms per dryer-day against a limit below 0.25, and a median lead time of 22 minutes against a target of at least 15.

Whether synthetic drift training could teach a model to ignore drift without hiding slow faults was uncertain. It was determined that this training hides slow faults, so it is the wrong approach here. The model had learned to treat slow rises as drift, so column plugs developing over 30 to 60 minutes went undetected. This resolved the uncertainty regarding drift tolerance versus slow-fault detection. Based on this understanding, the company dropped that approach and moved to the energy balance residual model.

The open question is single-sensor dryers, where false alarms are still above target. Without a redundant sensor, the bias tracker cannot separate drift from process change. In shadow mode these dryers gave 0.64 false alarms per dryer-day, and exhaust temperature as an indirect reference cut that to 0.33, against a limit below 0.25. Flame event lead time was 14 minutes on one event, under the 15-minute target. Moisture sensor drift, performance across a full season of live alerts, and whether 11 documented faults suffice for validation remain unresolved. A second field trial at the Ashgrove elevator is booked for spring 2027.

The project aimed to warn operators of burner and column faults early, without flooding them with false alarms. That goal was met on injected drift, with 10 of 11 faults caught, but it has not yet been shown in live alerts.

sections.s242:
Biofilm on the optical window of an in-line analyzer was the problem that drove this work, and the project was in no way routine. Port Aldous Instruments is a water-quality instrument developer that designs and builds in-line optical analyzers for municipal treatment plants. The company set out to build an analyzer that stays accurate for weeks without cleaning. Its main product line measures UV absorbance at 254 nm as a proxy for dissolved organic carbon. Customers want at least 30 days between cleanings with drift under 5 percent. The prior prototype, Orion-1, used a fused silica window with a mechanical wiper. It held calibration for only 14 days in secondary effluent before drift passed 5 percent.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to keep a UV window clear of biofilm was insufficient. Published coatings were biocidal, which is not permitted for this use, or lost 30 to 60 percent of transmission at 254 nm. Most fluoropolymers and hydrogels that resist fouling lose that share of transmission at 254 nm. No documented coating combined UV clarity with durability in chlorinated water. Existing understanding assumed fouling attenuates light evenly across wavelengths, although biofilm contains UV-absorbing organics. Published ultrasonic cleaning results were mixed, and its power draw of about 4 W exceeded the 1.5 W available.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of UV-transparent anti-fouling window coatings and dual-wavelength fouling compensation, for the purposes of creating an in-line analyzer with a coated window and a reference channel that holds drift under 5 percent for 30 days without cleaning.

It was uncertain whether any window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days while staying UV-clear at 254 nm, because published coatings were biocidal or lost 30 to 60 percent of transmission. It was uncertain whether a sol-gel layer with a fluorinated top surface would survive chlorine and grit, because scratches had given biofilm anchoring sites on Orion-1. It was uncertain whether 254 nm attenuation would stay a stable multiple of the 365 nm reference loss as the biofilm matured, because biofilm composition may change with age.
sections.s244:
The coupon screening addressed whether any window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days while staying UV-clear at 254 nm. This was open because published coatings were biocidal or lost 30 to 60 percent of transmission. The company planned coupon screening of four coatings against uncoated controls to find one that stays UV-clear and resists biofilm. The candidates were a fluorosilane monolayer, a sol-gel silica with a fluorinated top surface, a zwitterionic polymer brush and a thin titania film. The coating that passed would go into later bench and field work.

The hypothesis was that if a silica sol-gel has a fluorinated top surface, then raw drift stays under 5 percent for 30 days. Transmission at 254 nm would also stay at or above 85 percent when new. The test used 12 coupons of each coating against 12 uncoated controls for 42 days in a secondary effluent side stream. Transmission at 254 nm was measured every 3 days. Sol-gel coupons failing to reach 30 days under 5 percent loss would disprove the hypothesis.

The company coated fused silica coupons with the four candidates and exposed them alongside the controls. Controls lost 5 percent of transmission by day 11 and 22 percent by day 42. The fluorosilane monolayer started at 92 percent but lost 5 percent by day 17. The titania film grew biofilm faster than the controls. Suspected causes are in-stream UV too low to activate it and a rough surface aiding attachment, neither confirmed. The sol-gel with a fluorinated top started at 89 percent and lost 5 percent at day 31. Only this candidate met both targets, and only just.

The zwitterionic polymer brush showed the best biofilm resistance of the four, but it started at only 71 percent transmission. That was below the 85 percent target from day one, so it failed the clarity requirement. The most fouling-resistant coating tested was not UV-clear enough for 254 nm use.

Fouling on the sol-gel coupons began at the edges, where the coating was thinnest. The company reduced the dip withdrawal speed from 2 mm/s to 1 mm/s. This gave a more even layer of about 180 nm. A second round of 12 coupons ran in November 2025. Initial transmission dropped to 87 percent, still above target. Time to 5 percent loss rose from 31 to 38 days.

The remaining uncertainty was whether a fixed 254/365 nm attenuation multiple could correct fouling drift. The company logged both channels every 5 minutes on six Orion-2 heads with deliberately uncoated windows in a fouling tank. The tank used recirculated secondary effluent spiked with nutrients to speed biofilm growth about threefold. The run lasted 21 days, and a window was pulled every 3 days to measure the film directly. The multiple was about 1.6 in the first 4 to 5 days and fell to about 1.15 after about day 8. A fixed multiple of 1.4 left 4.8 percent drift at day 21, which disproved the fixed-ratio hypothesis.

The multiple tracked accumulated 365 nm loss. The company therefore fitted the correction factor as a function of that loss, using 4 heads and testing on the other 2. Corrected drift was 1.7 percent at day 21. A fresh 21-day test in January 2026 with 6 new heads gave 1.9 percent worst case. This met the 2 percent target on the bench.

Four complete Orion-2 units then ran at the Harbourside plant from February 9 to June 12 2026. Two ran on secondary effluent and two on chlorinated final effluent. On secondary effluent, raw drift crossed 5 percent at day 36 and day 40. Corrected drift stayed under 2 percent until day 52 and day 55. On final effluent, one coating thinned after about 70 days, with a 9 percent transmission drop between day 70 and day 90 that was not biofilm. Chlorine attack on the fluorinated layer is suspected but not confirmed.
sections.s246:
It was uncertain whether any window surface could resist biofilm for 30 days while staying UV-clear at 254 nm, and the work answered that only narrowly. The objective was to advance knowledge of UV-transparent anti-fouling coatings and dual-wavelength fouling compensation for an analyzer holding drift under 5 percent for 30 days. Of four candidates, only the sol-gel with a fluorinated top met both targets, and only just, starting at 89 percent transmission and losing 5 percent at day 31. The fixed-ratio hypothesis was disproved, and a fitted correction replaced it.

Through this investigation, it was established that the coatings that resist biofilm best are not UV-clear enough for 254 nm use. The zwitterionic brush resisted biofilm best but started at only 71 percent transmission, so it failed the 85 percent clarity target from day one. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether any surface could combine fouling resistance with UV clarity, given that published coatings were biocidal or lost 30 to 60 percent of transmission. Based on this understanding, the company narrowed development to the sol-gel, and a more even layer of about 180 nm extended time to 5 percent loss to 38 days at 87 percent initial transmission.

Coating durability in chlorinated water beyond 70 days remains unresolved. On one final effluent unit, transmission fell 9 percent between day 70 and day 90 without biofilm; chlorine attack on the fluorinated layer is suspected but not confirmed. Behaviour at 4 to 6 C is also unknown, since field data covered 9 to 17 C. Fiscal 2027 work will address chlorinated-water durability, winter conditions and transfer of the correction curve to a second plant.

The project goal was an analyzer running 30 days without cleaning. The sol-gel window on secondary effluent kept raw drift under 5 percent until day 36 and day 40, and corrected drift stayed under 2 percent until day 52 and day 55.

sections.s242:
Burr height on cast A357 aluminium could not be reliably estimated from fast 2D images, and no stable relationship was known between that height and the contact force needed to hold edge radius. The company designs and builds robotic finishing cells for aerospace and medical parts. It set out to build a robotic cell that deburrs cast aluminium brackets automatically inside the customer's 4-minute cycle. The company integrates industrial arms with its own tooling, fixturing and control software.

The limitations to standard practice were that the knowledge required to control edge radius on cast A357 brackets was insufficient. A fixed path at fixed force over-rounds small burrs or leaves large ones: a force high enough to remove a 1.2 mm burr over-rounds edges that had only 0.1 mm. No documented model related a given burr height and force to a resulting edge radius. Full 3D laser scanning gives burr height but takes about 90 seconds per bracket, too long for the cycle.

The technological objective was to advance the understanding of whether burr height on cast aluminium can be estimated from 2D images accurately and fast enough. It also sought to understand how that height relates to compliant spindle force. The purpose was to create an adaptive robotic deburring cell that holds edge radius at 0.2 to 0.5 mm within a 4-minute cycle.

It was uncertain whether burr height could be estimated from 2D images with enough accuracy and speed on cast aluminium, because nobody had done this on a surface that is shiny in places and dull in others, with burrs small relative to the part. The burr shows as a small shadow or bright line depending on lighting angle. It was also uncertain whether that appearance could be linked to actual height, because the link depends on burr shape, which varies. Whether a stable relationship existed between burr height and compliant spindle force, despite casting variation, also remained open.
sections.s244:
The technological problem was whether burr height on cast A357 brackets could be estimated from fast 2D images, and whether that estimate could set a contact force on the compliant spindle that holds edge radius at 0.2 to 0.5 mm. The team planned a fixed-force baseline first, then a vision estimate checked against a laser profiler. Each step answered one uncertainty from Line 242. The baseline measured the limit of standard practice. The profiler comparison tested estimation accuracy and speed. Later force-map trials tested the height-to-force relationship. All work ran in the Bay 4 pilot cell on brackets from three casting lots.

It was hypothesized that if burr height were estimated within 0.1 mm RMS in under 120 ms per edge, and the compliant spindle force were set from that estimate, then edge radius would stay within 0.2 to 0.5 mm on at least 97 percent of edges and the reject rate would fall below 3 percent within a 4-minute cycle. A miss on either estimation target, or a force relationship too unstable to control, would disprove it.

The company first needed a baseline, because it was unknown how a fixed force would perform on casting variation. It ran 120 brackets with the compliant spindle at a fixed 20 N on a fixed path. Cycle time was 3 min 10 s, but 14 percent of brackets were rejected. About two thirds of the rejects were leftover burrs on high-burr edges. The rest were edges over-rounded beyond 0.5 mm where burrs were small. This confirmed that one force cannot serve both burr extremes, so per-edge force needed a burr height estimate.

Nobody had estimated burr height from 2D images on cast aluminium, so accuracy and speed were unknown. The company imaged 400 edges with one 12 MP camera and a low-angle ring light, and compared each estimate with a laser profiler reference. Single-angle vision gave 0.18 mm RMS at about 210 ms per edge, missing both targets. Specular reflection on machined faces made some burrs look taller, and 31 of 400 edges were overestimated by more than 0.4 mm. A borrowed structured light 3D camera was then tried. Its depth resolution was about 0.2 mm at roughly 400 ms per capture, so work returned to 2D imaging.

The burr shows as a small shadow or bright line depending on lighting angle, and its link to actual height depends on burr shape, which varies. The company therefore took two shots per edge with lights at 15 and 60 degrees and applied two-angle differencing. It cropped each image around the edge from the CAD path and processed it on a GPU. On the same 400 edges, error fell to 0.07 mm RMS at 95 ms per edge, meeting both targets. The worst single-edge error was 0.19 mm. Two-angle differencing removed the reflection failure.

Whether a stable relationship existed between burr height and force was still unknown. The company cut 60 coupons from scrap brackets with burrs of 0.1 to 1.2 mm, applied forces of 8 to 40 N, and measured the resulting radius. The relationship was non-linear: about 10 to 22 N covered burrs of 0.1 to about 0.6 mm, then about 34 N was needed at 1.2 mm. A lookup table built from this force map, run on 300 brackets, gave 4.3 percent rejects, 96.1 percent of edges in window and 3 min 50 s. Most rejects were on 2.5 mm thin flanges. Above about 28 N the flange flexed and the compliant spindle chattered.

Raising force on thin flanges failed, so the company capped force at 26 N and slowed feed from 40 to 25 mm/s. A second pass on 40 brackets gave 3.9 percent rejects. On 360 brackets with slower feed, chatter disappeared, with 2.6 percent rejects, 97.8 percent of edges in window and 3 min 58 s. Force had to be traded for dwell time on thin walls.

Finally, over about 150 brackets, the removal rate of the compliant spindle dropped as the abrasive wore, and radius drifted smaller. Every 25 brackets, the cell deburred and imaged a reference coupon and scaled the force map up. With this correction, 240 brackets gave 2.4 percent rejects and no drift trend.
sections.s246:
Our objective was to learn whether burr height on cast A357 aluminium can be estimated from fast 2D images, and whether that estimate can set contact force on the compliant spindle. The hypothesis was partly proven. Two-angle imaging cut error to 0.07 mm RMS and processing to 95 ms per edge, inside the 0.1 mm and 120 ms targets. The force relationship was mapped, but the full reject and edge-window targets were reached only after further changes.

Through systematic investigation, we found that specular reflection on machined faces was the main cause of single-angle burr height error. The burr shows as a small shadow or bright line depending on lighting angle, and its link to actual height depends on burr shape, which varies. Reflection made some burrs look taller: 31 of 400 edges were overestimated by more than 0.4 mm. We established that two-angle differencing separates burr shadow from face reflection and removed that failure. This resolved the uncertainty regarding whether 2D estimation could be accurate and fast enough on shiny cast aluminium. Based on this understanding, we used lights at 15 and 60 degrees with GPU processing to feed the force map.

The cell remains at pilot stage. Whether the method transfers to other alloys without redoing the whole force map is untested. We built the force map on A357, and removal behaviour at a given force is expected to depend on the material. We plan to assess how much of the existing map carries over before any new mapping.

The knowledge gained moves the project toward its goal of a robotic cell that deburrs cast brackets to a 0.2 to 0.5 mm edge radius within a 4-minute cycle. Two-angle imaging gave burr height at 0.07 mm RMS, inside the 0.1 mm goal. Processing took 95 ms per edge, under the 120 ms target, and replaced a 90-second laser scan. Force can now be set per edge rather than fixed for the whole path.

notes: 2026-10-02: added after alert 7 on the /alerts board (1 September). A writer uploaded a detailed PD Writing Customized Settings document before the first draft, chat listed 16 places where the draft deviated, and the second draft still deviated after a bulk revision. The owner chose a sixth fixture that measures how well a draft follows a writer's settings document, scored automatically.

The settings document is uploaded as Writer's Notes (category writer_notes) by the reviewer account the suite acts as. That account has an internal role, so documentTrust gives it internal trust, and its first line matches the settings title the product detects. Its word caps are written so the product's own rule extraction reads them; the fixture check proves both.

The scripted writer makes no decision of its own: the first Seed on each step, approve, sign off. Previous-year status is skipped because the project started in July 2025. So the fixture measures the settings document, not the writer's choices.

Automatic checks added for this fixture: the settings document was applied as the Writer Profile; each required term is used and its synonyms are absent; no banned word or phrase; the required openings; each Line within its settings word cap; no excluded work mentioned (a heuristic); no first person; settings rules broken, N of M, per Line and overall; and the Compliance Note rows that mention the settings document or the Writer Profile. The pack also lists every settings rule per Line. No earlier check was removed or weakened.

Review fixes (2026-10-02, lead review, Claude Opus 5.5): one matcher for every term, synonym, banned phrase and exclusion marker. It matches whole words in any case, a space or a hyphen between words, and the last word singular or with s or es, so "DFTs", "substrate temperatures", "edge-wrap" and "dry-film thickness" are breaks and "outgassing defect rate" uses "outgassing defects". Every scored synonym is one the settings document names.

The settings document says never to write pinholes, pinholing, blisters or blistering on their own, so one of them in a sentence that also says outgassing defects is not a break (allowedWithTerm). A banned word counts only in the forms listed: "break-through" is the MEK test term ("no break-through to the board"), not "breakthrough", and "successful" and "unsuccessfully" are not counted as forms of "successfully". The judges decide whether such a word breaks the rule.

Known limitation (2026-10-05, amendment 2026-10-04 first, Round 4): the datasheet steel error recurs in all five runs of this fixture. The analysis step merges "Normal powder for steel cures at 160 to 200 C" into the datasheet claim, and the Technological limitations Seed says the datasheets were developed for flat steel (run 3: "flat steel or thin panels") while quoting the steel sentence, so the word-level quote checks see support. The sources say only that the datasheet number is for flat panels. Follow-up for the owner to decide: a meaning-level check of each Seed claim against its own quote.

Greptile on PR #27 (2026-10-05): the document bans "optimize" in any form, and the matcher counts only the listed forms plus an s or es ending, so "optimize" lists every form of the word: optimise, optimized, optimised, optimizing, optimising, optimization, optimisation, optimizer, optimiser, optimizable and optimisable (with s or es, so optimizers and optimizations count too). "Optimal" and "optimum" are other words, not forms of it. The other banned entries have no other forms the matcher misses ("trial-and-error" and "industry leading" match through the hyphen or space rule), and the choice above about "successful" and "break-through" stands.

sections.s242:
The company finishes MDF panels for other companies, such as cabinet doors, and had run no powder panels before July 2025. Supplier datasheets for low-temperature powder are written for thin flat panels, not 25 mm routed doors. Making the board conductive enough for powder to stick and curing the powder both rely on heat, and heat drives moisture and resin vapour out of the MDF as outgassing defects. The moisture that gives conductivity is the same moisture that outgasses.

The aim of this work was to powder coat 25 mm routed MDF doors for customers, by finding a heat setting that gave conductivity and cure below the outgassing onset. Targets were edge coverage of at least 60 microns, at most 1 outgassing defect per square metre, a panel surface temperature of 120 C or less, a cure window at least 8 C wide, and a line speed of 2.5 m per minute.

It was not known at the outset whether conductivity and full cure could both be reached below outgassing onset. Preheat is heat, so no setting was known to do both. It also remained uncertain whether any low-temperature powder could cure there with a usable cure window, and whether the deep cove profile could reach the same edge coverage as the faces.
sections.s244:
The company ran five trials from August 2025 to June 2026, logging panel surface temperature with thermocouples on every test panel and changing one variable at a time. The hypothesis was that if an edge sealer replaces preheat, then edge coverage reaches 60 microns below outgassing onset.

Trial 1 followed the supplier datasheet: infrared preheat to 110 C, a standard low-temperature powder and 10 minutes in a 135 C convection oven. Panel surface temperature reached 131 C. Outgassing defects averaged 14 per square metre overall and 30 per square metre on the routed edges. Edge film build was 35 microns against 82 microns on the faces. Cure measured 55 to 62 MEK rubs. The datasheet process did not transfer to 25 mm routed MDF.

Trial 2 kept the preheat and lowered oven air to 125 C, then raised it to 127 C. The team ran several dwell times to test whether dwell time controlled outgassing onset. Onset did not move with dwell time and stayed at about 118 to 122 C, so peak panel surface temperature, not dwell time, was the controlling variable. At 125 C air, defects were 4 per square metre but cure was only 30 MEK rubs, so the cure window was close to zero.

Trial 3 applied a water-based conductive edge sealer to the routed edges only and cut preheat from 110 C to 85 C. Edge coverage averaged 58 microns (minimum 47) and defects fell to 1.8 per square metre. Overspray on the faces gave 3B adhesion on 12 percent of panels against a 5B target; an edge-only nozzle and a face mask returned it to 5B.

Trial 4 combined the edge sealer with a polyester-epoxy hybrid powder at three catalyst levels. The fastest level cut gel time from 210 s to 95 s at 125 C and reached full cure at 120 C in 9 minutes. The cure window was 113 to 121 C. On 140 panels, edge coverage averaged 64 microns (minimum 52) and defects were 0.6 per square metre.

Trial 5 ran 600 doors on customer orders over three weeks. Defects averaged 0.9 per square metre and MEK passed on 98 percent of panels. The failures all came from one batch when oven zone 3 drifted 6 C low. Shaker doors averaged 0.8 defects per square metre with none below 60 microns edge coverage. On deep cove doors, 13 percent fell below 60 microns. Whether a different sealer, gun angle or cove geometry would bring the cove interior to 60 microns is not yet known. Shaker doors are ready for production; deep cove coverage and oven zone control remain open for fiscal 2027 trials.
sections.s246:
The experimental work established that outgassing defects start at a panel surface temperature of about 118 to 122 C on 25 mm routed MDF, at every dwell time tried. Trial 2 ran several dwell times and the onset did not move, so peak panel surface temperature, not dwell time, was the controlling variable. This addressed the conflict stated at the outset: preheat is heat, and the moisture that gives conductivity is the same moisture that outgasses.

The company then separated conductivity from heat. An edge sealer cut preheat from 110 C to 85 C; edge coverage averaged 58 microns and outgassing defects fell to 1.8 per square metre. Fast-catalysed powder, with a gel time of 95 s at 125 C, reached full cure at a panel surface temperature of 120 C in 9 minutes. The cure window, mapped in 1 C steps, was 113 to 121 C, 8 C wide. On 140 panels, edge coverage averaged 64 microns and outgassing defects were 0.6 per square metre, the first time the cure and outgassing targets were met on the same panels. The fastest catalyst level gave orange peel of 5 against a target of 6.

Shaker doors are ready for production. Deep cove edge coverage is only partly met: 13 percent of deep cove panels fell below 60 microns in the pilot, and the cause and remedy are not yet known. Oven zone control also remains open.
